one_liner: Rust HTTP/1.1 web framework whose nio thread-per-core build out-served actix-web by ~11% on an empty-route benchmark.
what_it_does: Ohkami is a declarative Rust web framework. Routes are tuples like "/users/:id".GET(handler). Handlers are async fns that take typed extractors (Path, Query, Json, Context) and return IntoResponse types, and middleware ('fangs') attaches globally or per route. One Cargo feature picks the runtime: tokio, smol, nio, glommio, monoio, compio, Cloudflare Workers or AWS Lambda. It is not a drop-in for actix-web, because routing, extractors, middleware and app state all use different APIs, and it speaks only HTTP/1.1 (TLS, SSE and WebSocket are behind features).
how_it_is_fast: With rt_nio, the accept loop hands each connection to nio::spawn_pinned, which puts it on the least-loaded worker. conn.connect() then registers the socket with that worker's own mio reactor, so the connection's reads, writes and keep-alive timer stay on one thread with no work stealing, atomics or cross-thread wakeups (this is the 'thread-per-core' design in nio's announcement post). Ohkami's HTTP/1.1 path is its own code, not hyper: each connection reuses one 2 KiB read buffer, the request line and headers are parsed in place with header values borrowed as slices of that buffer, standard headers go in a byte-indexed fixed array, and routing uses a compressed radix tree of leaked static nodes. The tokio build runs the same request path on tokio's work-stealing scheduler and measured only ~3% over actix, so most of the margin follows the runtime choice.
when_to_use: Linux HTTP/1.1 REST/JSON services with small requests over keep-alive connections, where you want more req/s per core than actix-web or hyper and can accept a pre-1.0 framework.
Handlers that are short and similar in cost, so pinning each connection to one nio worker (no migration, no stealing) does not create hot threads.
One handler/middleware codebase that must run on native servers, Cloudflare Workers (wasm32) and AWS Lambda, or where you want OpenAPI generated from handler types without macros.
When you will benchmark rt_nio against rt_tokio on your own traffic. Switching is one Cargo feature plus the main attribute (#[nio::main] vs #[tokio::main]).
when_not_to_use: You need HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 (README: not supported; TLS is HTTP/1.1-only), chunked request bodies (issue #583, open), or HTTP/1.0 clients (the reader requires 'HTTP/1.1' and answers 505).
CPU-heavy or uneven handlers on rt_nio. Pinned connections never move to another worker, so one slow handler stalls every connection on its worker. Tokio's work stealing is the safer default here.

Tail latency matters more than peak req/s. At c=512 ohkami-nio had a lower median than actix (2.45 vs 3.13 ms) but a higher p99 (3.94 vs 3.22 ms) and about 6x the standard deviation (1.08 vs 0.18 ms).

You need actix-web's maturity. Ohkami is 0.24.x with breaking renames queued (fang->middleware, claw->handler::component; issues #602/#603), has ~1.6k crates.io downloads in the last 90 days, and nio is a 0.1.x runtime (first stable release Jan 2026, ~7.7k downloads) with one listed author.
Choosing rt_smol for speed. smol::spawn runs on smol's global executor, which is single-threaded unless SMOL_THREADS is set. In the benchmark the smol build reached 53,077 req/s on ~1.15 of 4 cores.

integration.dependencies: ohkami_lib, ohkami_macros, byte_reader, serde, serde_json, http, base64, hmac, sha2, uuid, plus exactly one runtime crate chosen by feature (rt_nio pulls nio 0.1.3 with tokio-io traits; nio itself uses mio and crossbeam). Optional: rustls + anysc-rustls (tls), mews (ws), ohkami_openapi (openapi), tracing.
integration.min_toolchain: Rust edition 2024. README MSRV is 'latest stable', and CI runs stable and nightly. The benchmark built with Rust 1.98.
integration.platforms: Native runtimes: CI runs only on ubuntu-latest for both ohkami and nio (mio-based); other OSes not documented. Also wasm32 via rt_worker (Cloudflare Workers) and AWS Lambda via rt_lambda.
integration.thread_safety: On tokio, smol and lambda builds the compiler enforces Send + Sync + 'static on handlers and fangs. On rt_nio those bounds are dropped, but the router is shared across nio worker threads through an unsafe impl Send/Sync, so keeping handler and Context state thread-safe is up to you.

gotchas: rt_nio soundness hole: SendSyncOnThreaded becomes a blanket impl when __rt_threaded__ is off, yet nio_rt.rs does 'unsafe impl Send/Sync for Router' and spawns sessions on several workers. Handler or Context state built on Rc, RefCell or Cell compiles and can race.

The native reader does one read() per request into the fixed buffer (request_bufsize, default 2 KiB) and parses only what arrived. A request head larger than the buffer or split across reads fails with 431 (raise OHKAMI_REQUEST_BUFSIZE). It also requires exactly ': ' after each header name, and bytes of a pipelined second request in the same read are zeroed, not queued.

Router construction leaks memory on purpose (Vec::leak for route nodes and allowed-method strings; issue #643, open). That is harmless for one long-lived server but accumulates if you rebuild Ohkami instances in-process (tests, hot reload).
GET, HEAD and OPTIONS requests with a nonzero Content-Length are rejected with 400. Config::default() ignores the OHKAMI_* environment overrides; use Config::new() if you want them.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: In the same 2026-09-24 run, ohkami-nio (181.8k req/s at c=512) trailed may_minihttp (194.4k) but beat the C/C++ siblings measured there: CWIST 151.3k, Agoo-C 149.2k, Drogon 131.6k. Pick ohkami over may_minihttp when you need its framework layer (typed extractors, fangs, TLS, WebSocket, OpenAPI, Workers/Lambda targets), and over the C/C++ entries when you want a Rust codebase.
verified_claims_summary: In the-benchmarker/web-frameworks develop-branch data.json (2026-09-24; zrk --closed, GET / with an empty body, keep-alive, 15 s), the server container was pinned to ~4 cores (98.7-98.8% CPU saturation for both frameworks) on a host whose metadata reads both 'M1 Eight-Core Processor' and x86_64. There, ohkami 0.24 on nio did 181,797 req/s at c=512 vs actix-web 4.8 at 163,415 (+11%), with +2.7% at c=64 and +11.6% at c=256; both were built with Rust 1.98, fat LTO, codegen-units=1 and panic=abort. The ohkami tokio build was only +3%, and the older master-branch data.json (updated 2026-09-20, an earlier method revision) had ohkami-nio behind actix (74,657 vs 99,835 req/s at c=512; 84,831 vs 115,638 at c=64), so the nio lead depends on the load model.
status_note: Actively maintained (last commit 2026-08-25; latest crates.io release 0.24.9 on 2026-04-12, 78 versions since 2022) and MIT-licensed as an ordinary crate, but still pre-1.0 with open breaking-change issues. The nio runtime behind the headline number is Apache-2.0 and 0.1.x.
